title: Ensure Model Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability
intro: Protecting models themselves: keeping weights, methods and other model IP confidential; preventing extraction through the API; watermarking and fingerprinting models to prove ownership and trace leaks; preserving integrity with hashing, signing and version control; and keeping AI services available with rate limits, quotas and graceful degradation.
objectives: Identify the components of model IP and apply layered controls to keep model weights confidential
Explain model extraction at a high level and reduce its risk with access control, output minimisation, rate limits and detection
Distinguish model watermarking from fingerprinting, and use them for ownership evidence and leak tracing
Preserve model integrity with hashing, signing, safe formats, verification points and version control
Keep AI services available with token-aware rate limits, quotas, budget caps and graceful degradation that fails safe

sections.title: Model confidentiality: weights, algorithms and IP

scenes.title: Your model is the asset
scenes.sub: Protecting weights, algorithms and intellectual property
scenes.say: A trained model concentrates months of compute, proprietary data and hard-won expertise into a set of files. Anyone who copies those files has the model. | This video covers model confidentiality: protecting the weights, the methods and prompts around them, and the intellectual property they represent.

scenes.title: What needs protecting
scenes.say: Model intellectual property is more than one file. | The weights: the trained parameters themselves, and the most valuable target. | The architecture, training code, hyperparameters and methods. | The data pipelines and curation choices behind the training data, which are often the hardest part to replicate. | Fine-tuned versions and adapters, which are small files that carry a lot of value. | System prompts and configuration, which should be protected, but designed on the assumption that they can leak. | And evaluation suites and red-team findings, which would give an attacker a map of the model’s weaknesses.

scenes.title: Layered protection for model weights
layers: Least privilege, JIT and two-person export
Encryption with keys in an HSM
scenes.say: Protecting weights takes layers, because the threats are varied. | Classification as highly restricted, with access on a need-to-know basis, stops weights being shared too widely in the first place. | Least privilege, just-in-time access, and a two-person rule for exporting weights stop a single rogue or compromised account from downloading them. | Encryption at rest, with keys held in a hardware security module, makes a stolen backup or disk useless. | And isolated training and serving networks, with egress monitoring, catch large transfers of model files leaving the environment.

scenes.title: Closed and open weights
scenes.say: Confidentiality depends on how a model is released. | Closed weights stay with the developer. Open weights can be downloaded by anyone. | For closed weights, the main risks are theft, insiders and extraction through the API. For open weights, confidentiality is given up by design, and the risk shifts to misuse. | Closed weights rely on access control, encryption and monitoring. Open releases rely on licence terms and careful review before release. | And safeguards on a closed model are enforced on the server, while those built into open weights can be removed by fine-tuning. Once released, weights can’t be recalled.

scenes.title: Models outside your walls

items.d: Can be pulled from the app

scenes.say: Models increasingly run outside environments you fully control. | Models shipped inside mobile or desktop apps can be extracted by anyone with the device. Encrypt them with hardware-backed keys and accept some residual risk, but don’t ship your most valuable models this way. | In third-party clouds, confidential computing with remote attestation can protect weights while they are in use. | For partners and researchers, offer controlled access through an API or secure environment rather than handing over copies. | And on shared accelerators, isolate tenants and make sure memory is cleared between workloads.

items: Protect weights, methods, data pipelines, adapters, prompts and evaluations
Layer classification, access control, encryption and monitoring
Open release gives up confidentiality for good
Give access rather than copies; protect models in use
scenes.say: To recap. | Model IP includes weights, methods, data pipelines, adapters, prompts and evaluation results. | Protect weights in layers: classification, least privilege, encryption and egress monitoring. | Releasing weights openly gives up confidentiality for good. | And where you can, give partners access rather than copies, and protect models while they are in use.

blocks.md:
### What model IP includes
| Asset | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Weights** | The trained model itself; with the weights and the architecture, anyone can run it |
| **Architecture, code and training recipes** | Hyperparameters, data mixtures and methods represent research investment |
| **Training data and curation pipelines** | Often the real competitive advantage, and may contain personal or licensed data |
| **Fine-tunes and adapters** | Small files (such as LoRA adapters) that encode valuable domain knowledge |
| **System prompts and configuration** | Product behaviour and guardrail settings; OWASP lists system prompt leakage as LLM07:2025, so never put secrets in them |
| **Evaluation suites and red-team findings** | Reveal weaknesses and how to exploit them |

**Legal angle:** model weights and methods are often protected as **trade secrets**, and trade secret protection generally requires *reasonable measures* to keep the information secret. Access controls, NDAs and need-to-know practices therefore protect the legal position as well as the asset. Code is protected by copyright; the legal status of weights themselves is less settled.

### Threats to model confidentiality
- **External theft:** intrusion into training clusters, registries, storage or MLOps tooling, or compromise of a supplier.
- **Insiders:** employees, contractors and departing staff with access to weights or recipes.
- **Misconfiguration:** publicly readable buckets, open model servers and leaked tokens.
- **Extraction through the API:** copying functionality through queries (Section 2).
- **Over-broad distribution:** in March 2023, Meta’s LLaMA weights, shared with approved researchers, appeared on a public forum within about a week. Every copy you hand out is a copy you no longer control.
- **Side channels and shared hardware:** weak tenant isolation on shared accelerators and memory not cleared between workloads.
- **On-device extraction:** reverse-engineering models shipped in apps.

### Controls
- **Inventory and classify** models, adapters and checkpoints; treat frontier or high-value weights as the most sensitive data you hold.
- **Access control:** least privilege, just-in-time access, phishing-resistant MFA, a **two-person rule** for exporting weights, and separate roles for training and serving.
- **Encryption** at rest and in transit, with customer-managed keys in HSMs, and envelope encryption for large checkpoints (Module 3.4).
- **Confidential computing** for training or inference on infrastructure you don’t control: trusted execution environments, including GPU confidential computing modes, with remote attestation before keys are released.
- **Network isolation:** no direct internet egress from training clusters, allow-listed destinations, and segmented model storage.
- **Monitoring:** alert on bulk downloads, unusual access to model stores, and large outbound transfers, including DLP rules for model file types and sizes.
- **Secure deletion** of superseded checkpoints and temporary copies (Module 3.4).
- **People and contracts:** NDAs, IP assignment, offboarding that revokes access promptly, and supplier security requirements.

The RAND Corporation’s 2024 report *Securing AI Model Weights* identified 38 distinct attack vectors and proposed five security levels, from protection against opportunistic attackers up to well-resourced nation states. Most organisations won’t need the highest levels, but the principle carries over: **protection should scale with the model’s value and its potential for misuse**.

blocks.title: Access, not copies
blocks.md: When a scenario involves sharing a valuable model with partners, researchers or customers, the strongest answer usually **provides access without handing over the weights**: a controlled API, a hosted secure environment or confidential computing. NDAs and watermarks help with deterrence and evidence, but they don’t prevent a copy from leaking.

q.q: A company plans to give 20 research partners copies of its proprietary model weights, under NDA, so they can evaluate the model. What is the BEST way to keep the weights confidential?
o: Rely on the NDA, which gives the company legal recourse if any partner leaks the weights
Give partners controlled access through an API or a secure environment, instead of copies
Encrypt each copy with a password, and send the password to partners in a separate email
Watermark each copy before sending it, so that any leak can be traced back to one partner
q.why: Not distributing the weights removes the risk of copies leaking. NDAs and watermarks deter and help prove a leak afterwards, and a password shared with each partner protects nothing once the copy is decrypted.

blocks.title: Stealing a model through the front door

scenes.title: Stealing a model through the front door
scenes.sub: How extraction works, and how to make it costly and visible
scenes.say: An attacker doesn’t need your weights to copy your model. With enough queries, they can train their own model on your model’s answers. | This video explains model extraction at a high level, and the layered controls that make it expensive and easy to spot.

scenes.title: How model extraction works
scenes.say: Here is the idea, at a high level. An attacker, often spread across many accounts, wants a copy of your model. | They send large numbers of chosen queries, designed to cover the range of inputs the model handles. | Your API answers every one, as it is designed to. | The answers become a free, labelled training set. | And the attacker trains a substitute model that behaves much like yours. They gain your capability without your costs, and a private copy on which to develop attacks that may then work against the original.

scenes.title: Less detail per answer raises the cost
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative relative number of queries an attacker needs
scenes.say: One of the most effective controls is simply returning less. In this illustrative chart, each step down in output detail raises the number of queries an attacker needs. | Full probability scores for every class reveal the most about the model’s decision boundaries. Returning only the top few, or a rounded top score, reveals less. | Returning just the label reveals the least. So give each use case only the detail it actually needs.

scenes.title: Make extraction expensive and visible

items.d: Ban training on outputs; act on abuse

scenes.say: No single control stops extraction, because anything a legitimate user can query, an attacker can approximate. The goal is to make it expensive and visible. | Authenticate every caller, and tie keys to verified customers, with no anonymous high-volume access. | Minimise outputs: labels instead of full scores, rounded confidence, and limited log-probabilities. | Apply rate limits and quotas per key, per user and per organisation. | Detect suspicious patterns, such as high volume, systematic coverage of the input space, and synthetic-looking queries, including across linked accounts. | Prohibit training on your outputs in your terms of service, and act on abuse. | And mark your model and outputs, so a copy can be identified later.

items: Extraction copies a model through its own API
Return only the detail each use case needs
Authenticate, rate-limit and set quotas per identity
Detect probing; back it with terms, watermarks and fingerprints
scenes.say: To recap. | Extraction copies a model through its own API, by training a substitute on its answers. | Return only the detail each use case needs. | Authenticate callers, and apply rate limits and quotas to every identity. | And detect probing patterns, backed by terms of service, watermarks and fingerprints.

blocks.md:
### What extraction targets
- **Functionality:** a substitute model that reproduces the target’s behaviour on the inputs that matter. For language models, this includes **distillation**: training a smaller model on a larger model’s outputs, which many providers’ terms prohibit for competing models.
- **Parameters:** simple models can sometimes be recovered almost exactly. Tramèr and colleagues (2016) showed that models behind commercial prediction APIs could be extracted with surprisingly few queries when confidence scores were returned. In 2024, Carlini and colleagues recovered part of the final layer of production OpenAI models through their API for a small cost, and the providers added mitigations.
- **Hyperparameters, architecture and decision boundaries**, which make further attacks easier.

### Why it matters
- **IP and revenue:** your capability, without your training costs.
- **Attack staging:** a local copy lets attackers craft evasion inputs and jailbreaks offline, which often **transfer** to the original model.
- **Privacy:** a copy can be probed without rate limits for memorised training data (Module 3.3).
- **Safety:** the copy carries none of your server-side safeguards.

Module 6.1 covers extraction alongside the other adversarial ML attacks, such as evasion, inversion and membership inference.

### Layered defences
| Layer | Controls |
|---|---|
| **Access** | Authenticate all calls; tie keys to verified customers; no anonymous high-volume access; stronger checks for high-risk features such as log-probabilities or embeddings |
| **Output minimisation** | Return labels rather than full probability vectors; round or bucket confidence scores; limit the number of log-probabilities returned and features such as logit bias; don’t expose embeddings or hidden states unless needed |
| **Rate limits and quotas** | Per key, user, organisation and IP range, with daily and monthly caps (Section 5) |
| **Detection** | Baseline normal use; flag high volume, broad or systematic coverage of the input space, unnatural or synthetic queries, and similar patterns spread across linked accounts; send alerts to the SOC (Module 5.3) |
| **Response** | Throttle, require step-up verification, suspend accounts, and pursue contractual or legal remedies |
| **Legal** | Terms of service that prohibit using outputs to train competing models, and API agreements with audit rights |
| **Evidence** | Model watermarks and fingerprints, so a suspected copy can be tested (Section 3) |

Research defences, such as perturbing returned probabilities, can raise extraction costs but also degrade answers for legitimate users. Treat them as optional extras, after access control, output minimisation, rate limiting and detection.

blocks.title: Extraction questions
blocks.md: The best answers **reduce what each query reveals** and **limit and watch who queries**. Encrypting the weights doesn’t help, because extraction never touches them. Watermarks and terms of service support evidence and deterrence, but they don’t prevent extraction.

blocks.title: Which control is this?
pairs: The API returns only the top label instead of every class score
Output minimisation
Each key may send at most 600 requests and 200,000 tokens a minute
Rate limiting
An alert fires when one customer’s queries systematically sweep the input space
Query-pattern detection
The terms of service forbid using responses to train a competing model
Contractual deterrence
Secret prompts with planted answers are trained into the model
Trigger-set watermark (Section 3)

q.q: An image-classification API returns the full probability vector for all 1,000 classes with every answer. Which change MOST reduces what an extraction attacker learns from each query, while keeping the service useful?
o: Encrypt the model weights at rest with a customer-managed key held in an HSM
Return only the top label with a rounded confidence score, unless a customer needs more
Move the model to a different region, with a separate endpoint for each customer
Publish a prominent notice that copying the model breaches the terms of service for the API
q.why: Output minimisation directly reduces the information each query leaks about the decision boundary. Encryption protects stored weights, not the API; moving regions changes nothing; terms deter but don’t limit what is revealed.

scenes.title: Proving a model is yours
scenes.sub: Watermarks and fingerprints for models and their outputs
scenes.say: If a competitor launches a model that behaves suspiciously like yours, how would you prove it was copied? And which of your licensees leaked it? | This video covers model watermarking and fingerprinting: ways to mark and identify models, and their outputs, so ownership and origin can be checked.

scenes.title: Watermarks and fingerprints
rows: Identifying a model or a copy
scenes.say: The two terms overlap, but the core difference is simple. | A watermark is a hidden signal you deliberately embed. A fingerprint is a characteristic you use to identify a model. | Watermarking changes the model, or the way it generates output. Passive fingerprinting needs no change at all, though you can also embed a different fingerprint in each copy you distribute. | Watermarks are used to prove ownership and to mark generated content. Fingerprints identify which model, or which copy, you are looking at. | For example: a watermark might be a set of secret inputs with unusual expected answers, while a fingerprint might be unique to each licensee’s copy.

scenes.title: Verifying ownership with a trigger set
scenes.say: Here is one common ownership watermark, called a trigger set. The owner creates a set of secret inputs, each paired with an unusual answer that no independent model would give. | These pairs are trained into the model alongside its normal data, without affecting ordinary accuracy. | The model is released or deployed, and the trigger set is kept secret. | Later, a suspect model appears. The owner queries it with the triggers. | If it gives the planted answers far more often than chance would explain, that is strong evidence it was derived from the original.

scenes.title: Where watermarks and fingerprints help

items.d: Evidence that a model was copied
A unique copy for each licensee
Is this the version we approved?

scenes.say: These techniques support four practical goals. | In ownership disputes, they provide evidence that a model was copied or derived. | When a model is licensed to several parties, a unique fingerprint in each copy shows which one leaked. | Output watermarks mark generated text, images and audio as AI-made, which Module 2.6 covers for transparency. | And behavioural fingerprints help confirm that a hosted model is the version you approved.

scenes.title: Know the limits
scenes.say: Watermarks and fingerprints have real limits. | Determined attackers can remove or weaken them, by fine-tuning a stolen model, paraphrasing watermarked text, or distilling a new model from outputs. | Detection can produce false positives, so treat results as evidence alongside logs and contracts, not as proof on their own. | Watermark keys and trigger sets must stay secret, because an attacker who learns them can target them. | And with open weights, output watermarking built into the generation code can simply be switched off.

items: Watermarks are embedded; fingerprints identify
Trigger sets give evidence of copying
Unique per-copy fingerprints trace leaks
Signals can be degraded: combine with other evidence
scenes.say: To recap. | Watermarks are signals you embed; fingerprints are characteristics that identify a model or a copy. | Trigger sets give evidence that a suspect model was derived from yours. | Unique fingerprints in each distributed copy trace a leak to its source. | And because these signals can be degraded or removed, combine them with logs, contracts and other evidence.

blocks.md:
### Types and terms
| Technique | How it works | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **White-box model watermark** | A pattern embedded in the weights, readable by someone with the weights and the key | Proving ownership of a recovered copy of the weights |
| **Black-box (trigger-set) watermark** | Secret inputs trained to produce specific outputs; checked through queries alone | Testing a suspect model behind an API |
| **Output watermark** | A statistical signal in generated text (such as a subtle, keyed bias in word choice) or an imperceptible signal in images, audio or video | Marking content as AI-generated; tracing content to a model |
| **Passive fingerprint** | Characteristic responses or weight statistics that identify a model without changing it | Identifying which base model a product uses; detecting silent changes |
| **Active fingerprint (per copy)** | A different mark embedded in each distributed copy | Tracing which licensee’s copy leaked |

Examples include Google DeepMind’s SynthID, which watermarks generated text, images, audio and video, and **C2PA content credentials**, which attach signed provenance metadata rather than embedding a signal (Module 2.6). The two approaches complement each other: metadata is easily stripped, while watermarks survive some edits but can be degraded.

### Robustness and limits
- **Removal:** fine-tuning or pruning a stolen model can weaken weight and trigger-set watermarks; paraphrasing or translating text, and cropping or compressing images, can weaken output watermarks.
- **Distillation:** a substitute model trained on your outputs may not inherit trigger-set watermarks. Output watermarks, or fingerprints tuned to survive distillation, may still carry over.
- **False positives:** detectors produce errors, especially on short texts. Never base serious action, such as accusing a student or employee of using AI, on a detector score alone.
- **Key management:** watermark keys and trigger sets are secrets. Restrict access and keep verification in trusted hands.
- **Quality:** strong watermarks can slightly reduce output quality, so tune strength to the risk.

### Governance
- Decide which models get ownership watermarks, and whether distributed copies get per-licensee fingerprints.
- Record watermark and fingerprint details, and their keys, in the registry under restricted access.
- Keep supporting evidence such as training records, version history and access logs; it makes a watermark result far more persuasive in a dispute.
- Add output marking where transparency rules or policy require it (EU AI Act Article 50; Module 2.6).

q.q: A company licenses its proprietary model to five partners, and a copy later appears on a file-sharing site. Which technique would BEST have identified the partner whose copy leaked?
o: A single trigger-set watermark shared by all five copies of the model
A unique fingerprint embedded in each partner’s copy before it was distributed
A C2PA content credential attached to each output that the model generates
A SHA-256 hash of the model published on the company’s website at release
q.why: Per-licensee fingerprints make each copy distinguishable, so a leaked copy points to its source. A shared watermark proves ownership but not which copy leaked, credentials mark outputs, and one public hash can’t tell copies apart.

sections.title: Model integrity: hashing, signing and version control

blocks.title: Is this the model we approved?

scenes.title: Is this the model we approved?
scenes.say: Integrity means the model running in production is exactly the one you tested and approved, with nothing added, removed or swapped. | This video covers the controls that let you prove it: hashing, signing, version control, and verification at every hand-off.

scenes.title: Threats to model integrity

items.d: Unsafe formats run code on load

scenes.say: Integrity can be lost in several ways. | Weights can be tampered with after approval, for example to insert a backdoor. | Model files in unsafe serialisation formats can run code the moment they are loaded. | Artefacts can be swapped in storage or in the registry. | System prompts, configurations and guardrail settings can be changed without review. | Dependencies, adapters and container images can be compromised. | And a hosted model can change underneath you if you call an unpinned version.

scenes.title: Hash and sign once, verify everywhere
scenes.say: The pattern is: hash and sign once, then verify everywhere. A training run produces the model files. | Each file is hashed, and the digests are collected into a manifest, because a model is usually many files, not one. | The manifest is signed, using a key held in a hardware security module or a signing service tied to the pipeline’s verified identity. | The registry stores the signature and the provenance record. | The deployment gate verifies the signature and every digest, and refuses anything that doesn’t match. | And the serving runtime checks again when it loads the model, so files changed after deployment are caught too.

scenes.title: Hashes and signatures
scenes.say: Hashes and signatures do different jobs. | A hash proves the content hasn’t changed. A signature proves that too, and also who signed it. | A hash is only useful if the reference value is trusted. A signature relies on a trusted key or identity. | So an attacker who can replace both a file and its stored hash defeats a hash check, while defeating a signature requires stealing the signing key. | In practice, store digests in the registry, and sign a manifest of them, as the OpenSSF model signing specification does.

scenes.title: Version control for models

items.d: Any change makes a new version

scenes.say: Version control ties integrity to change management. | Make approved versions immutable: any change, however small, creates a new version. | Version everything that shapes behaviour together: weights, code, data references, prompts and configuration. | Put prompts and configuration under the same reviewed, protected change process as code. | Pin hosted models to dated versions rather than aliases that a provider can update. | And keep the full history, for rollback and for forensics after an incident.

items: Hash every file; sign the manifest
Verify at the deploy gate and again at load
Use safe formats; refuse unsigned models
Immutable, reviewed versions of everything that shapes behaviour
scenes.say: To recap. | Hash every model file, and sign the manifest with a protected key or verified identity. | Verify signatures and digests at the deployment gate, and again when the model loads. | Use safe file formats, and refuse unsigned models. | And keep immutable, reviewed versions of everything that shapes the model’s behaviour.

blocks.md:
### Hashing
- Use a strong cryptographic hash such as **SHA-256** (or SHA-3). MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance and must not be relied on against an adversary.
- A model package is usually many files (weight shards, tokenizer, configuration), so hash **every file** and record the digests in a **manifest**.
- A hash only proves integrity if the **reference value is trusted**: keep it in the registry, protected separately from the files, or bind it with a signature. A hash stored next to the file, with the same access rights, can be replaced along with the file.

### Signing and provenance
- **Digital signatures** bind the manifest to a signer. Keep signing keys in an HSM or KMS, or use **keyless signing** (for example, Sigstore), which issues short-lived certificates tied to a verified workload or person and records signatures in a public transparency log.
- The **OpenSSF Model Signing** specification (v1.0, 2025) defines how to sign model files and directories, building on Sigstore.
- **Provenance attestations** (for example, SLSA-style) record how a model was built: source, data references, pipeline and environment (Section 3 of Module 3.5).
- Sign **container images** for serving as well, and verify them at deployment.

### Verification points
1. **Registry intake:** reject artefacts without valid signatures and provenance.
2. **Deployment gate:** deploy only registry-approved versions whose signatures and digests verify (policy as code).
3. **Load time:** the serving runtime verifies before loading, and refuses on failure.
4. **Runtime monitoring:** file integrity monitoring on model storage, and periodic re-verification (Module 5.3).
5. **Third-party models:** verify publishers’ signatures and hashes before use (Module 3.7).

### Safe formats
Some serialisation formats, notably Python **pickle**, used by older PyTorch checkpoints, can execute arbitrary code when a file is loaded. Prefer **safetensors** or other formats that store only data, scan third-party files before loading, and never load untrusted pickles outside an isolated sandbox.

### Version control and configuration integrity
- The registry keeps **immutable versions**; Git holds code, prompts and configuration, with protected branches and peer review; data versions are recorded by reference or hash (Module 3.1).
- Treat **system prompts, guardrail rules and retrieval settings as code**: reviewed, versioned and deployed through the same pipeline.
- For **hosted models**, pin dated versions, track deprecations, and run a small set of canary prompts on a schedule to detect unannounced behaviour changes.
- Keep history for rollback (Module 3.5) and for incident investigation (Domain 5).

blocks.title: Integrity vocabulary
cards: The fixed-length output of a hash function. Any change to the input produces a different digest.
A list of every file in a model package with its digest, signed as a whole.
Short-lived certificates tied to a verified identity, with each signature recorded in a public transparency log.
Signed metadata describing how an artefact was built: source, inputs, pipeline and environment.
A data-only weight format that can’t execute code when it is loaded, unlike pickle.

q.q: A team stores a SHA-256 hash of each approved model file in the same storage bucket as the files, and checks it at deployment. Why is this weak against an attacker who gains write access to the bucket?
o: SHA-256 is too slow to compute on very large model files during deployment
The attacker can replace both the model and its stored hash, so the check still passes
Hashes can only ever detect accidental corruption in transit, never deliberate changes to files
SHA-256 is no longer considered collision-resistant for files of this size
q.why: A hash is only as trustworthy as its reference value. Keep digests in a separately protected registry and sign them, so an attacker who can change the files can’t also forge a valid reference.

sections.title: Model availability: rate limits, quotas and graceful degradation

scenes.title: Keeping the model up
scenes.sub: Rate limits, quotas and graceful degradation
scenes.say: AI services are expensive to run, and attackers know it. A flood of long prompts can exhaust GPUs, budgets or token quotas, and take a service down for everyone. | This video covers availability controls: rate limits, quotas and graceful degradation, so the service stays up and fails safely.

scenes.title: What threatens availability
scenes.say: OWASP calls this risk unbounded consumption, and it takes several forms. | Floods of requests: the classic denial of service. | Resource-heavy prompts: very long contexts, or requests for the maximum output length, where one request can cost as much as thousands of normal ones. | Runaway agents, stuck in loops of tool calls. | Denial of wallet: running up costs on pay-per-use services until budgets are exhausted. | Outages in dependencies, such as a model provider’s API or a vector database. | And contention for shared accelerators, where one workload starves another.

scenes.title: Layered limits
scenes.say: Availability controls work in layers. | Edge protection, with DDoS filtering and a web application firewall, absorbs volumetric floods before they reach your service. | Authentication and rate limits at the gateway stop anonymous scraping, and limit each identity’s requests and tokens per minute. | Quotas and budget caps limit what each user, team or application can consume per day or month, which stops denial of wallet. | And limits in the model server itself, on input and output length, concurrency and processing time, stop any single oversized request from monopolising capacity.

scenes.title: Rate limits, quotas and budget caps
scenes.say: Three related controls are easy to confuse. | A rate limit works over seconds or minutes. A quota works over days or months. A budget cap works over a billing period. | Rate limits protect capacity from bursts. Quotas enforce fair shares between users and teams. Budget caps protect spend. | Rate limits count requests and, for language models, tokens. Quotas count tokens or calls. Budget caps count money. | And when they are exceeded: a rate-limited caller is told to retry later, a caller over quota is blocked until the quota resets, and a budget cap raises alerts, then stops or degrades the service.

scenes.title: Degrade gracefully, and fail safe
scenes.say: When things go wrong, the service should degrade step by step, not collapse. Normally, requests go to the primary model. | If errors or latency cross a threshold, a circuit breaker trips and stops sending traffic to the failing dependency. | Requests move to a fallback model: smaller or from another provider, but assessed and approved in advance like any other model. | If that is unavailable too, the service offers reduced features, such as cached or core answers. | And as a last resort, users are routed to a non-AI path, such as a human queue or a simple form. | One rule overrides convenience: when a safety or security control, such as a content filter, is unavailable, the system should fail closed, holding or routing output for review rather than skipping the check.

items: Unbounded consumption: floods, heavy prompts, loops, cost
Layer edge, gateway, quota and server limits
Rate limits, quotas and budget caps do different jobs
Degrade step by step; security controls fail closed
scenes.say: To recap. | Unbounded consumption includes floods, resource-heavy prompts, runaway agents and cost exhaustion. | Layer the limits: edge protection, gateway rate limits, quotas and budgets, and server-side limits. | Rate limits, quotas and budget caps do different jobs, so use all three. | And degrade step by step when dependencies fail, while making sure that security and safety controls fail closed.

blocks.md:
### Unbounded consumption
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) lists **LLM10: Unbounded Consumption**: uncontrolled use that leads to denial of service, financial loss (denial of wallet), degraded service, or model theft through excessive querying (Section 2). Model-specific causes include variable-length input floods, very long contexts, requests for maximum-length outputs, recursive agent loops and resource-intensive multimodal inputs. Module 6.1 covers availability attacks, and Module 4.2 covers infrastructure-level controls against resource exhaustion, such as compute throttling and isolated accelerator capacity.

### Controls
| Control | Practice |
|---|---|
| **Input limits** | Maximum prompt tokens, file sizes, image resolutions and number of attachments |
| **Output limits** | Maximum output tokens per request, set to what the use case needs |
| **Rate limiting** | Requests *and tokens* per minute, per key, user, organisation and IP range; token-bucket or sliding-window algorithms; HTTP 429 responses with a Retry-After header |
| **Quotas** | Daily or monthly token and call allowances per user, team and application, with tiers for different customers |
| **Budget caps** | Spending alerts at thresholds, with hard caps that stop or degrade usage; separate budgets for experiments |
| **Server protection** | Timeouts, concurrency limits, request queues with priorities (so critical workloads keep capacity), and autoscaling with a **maximum**, so an attack can’t scale costs without limit |
| **Agent limits** | Maximum steps, tool calls, recursion depth, run time and cost per task, with loop detection |
| **Caching** | Reuse answers to repeated questions to reduce load |

### Resilience and graceful degradation
- **Circuit breakers** stop calling a failing dependency and retry it gradually, protecting both your service and the dependency.
- **Fallbacks:** a smaller or alternative model, or a second provider. A fallback must be assessed and approved like any other model, including data residency and contractual terms, so it can’t become a back door around governance.
- **Reduced modes:** cached answers, core features only, or longer response times instead of errors.
- **Non-AI paths:** a human queue, a standard form or an offline process for essential services.
- **Fail closed for security functions:** if a moderation, DLP or authorisation service is unavailable, hold or route outputs for review rather than skipping the check. Fail open only where the risk assessment accepts it.
- **Plan and test:** capacity planning, SLOs, load and stress testing (Module 4.4), multi-region deployment for critical services, and business continuity plans that map AI dependencies (Module 5.7).

blocks.title: Availability questions
blocks.md: Look for **token-aware** limits (request counts alone miss one huge prompt), **per-identity** quotas, **budget caps** for denial of wallet, and **graceful degradation**. When a security control such as a content filter fails, the best answer is usually to **fail closed**, not to keep serving unchecked output.

blocks.title: Match the control to the problem
pairs: One user sends 50 requests a second for a full minute
Rate limit
A team uses its whole month’s token allowance in a week
Quota
Spending on a pay-per-use API is heading for ten times the forecast
Budget cap
A provider’s API keeps timing out, and every call waits 60 seconds
Circuit breaker
The content filter is down, and replies are waiting to be checked
Fail closed

q.q: A customer-service LLM screens every reply through an external content-moderation API. The moderation API suddenly becomes unavailable. What should the system do?
o: Keep sending replies unmoderated, so that customers aren’t affected by the outage
Fail closed: hold replies or route them to human review until moderation is restored
Switch off logging for the outage, to reduce load on the remaining services
Retry each failed moderation call immediately until it succeeds, however long that takes
q.why: Moderation is a safety control, so it should fail closed: hold or route replies for review rather than releasing unchecked content. Failing open removes the control, switching off logging loses evidence, and endless immediate retries add load to a struggling dependency.

quiz.q: Why can strong access controls on model weights matter legally as well as technically?
o: They allow the weights to be patented once enough controls are in place
Trade secret protection usually requires reasonable steps to keep information secret
They transfer legal ownership of the weights from individual developers to the organisation
They make the model’s outputs exempt from data protection law in most jurisdictions
quiz.why: Trade secret protection usually requires reasonable secrecy measures, so access controls, NDAs and need-to-know practices support the legal position as well as security.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST reduces the risk of a single insider exporting a model’s weights?
o: Asking staff to sign an annual acceptable use statement that covers model files
A two-person rule and just-in-time access for exporting or downloading weights
Storing the weights in a different cloud region from the one used for training
Renaming the weight files so that they look like ordinary application log files
quiz.why: Requiring a second authorised person, and granting access only when needed, stops one rogue or compromised account acting alone. Statements, regions and renaming don’t restrict access.

quiz.q: What should be assumed about a production system prompt?
o: It is fully protected, because users can’t see it anywhere in the interface
It may leak, so it must not hold secrets or be the only security control
It is encrypted by the model provider, so it can safely hold API keys
It is ignored by the model whenever a user gives conflicting instructions
quiz.why: System prompts can often be extracted (OWASP LLM07:2025). Keep credentials out of them, and enforce security in controls outside the model.

quiz.q: What does a model extraction attack MAINLY produce?
o: A copy of the training data, recovered record by record from the provider’s storage
A substitute model that imitates the target, trained on the target’s own answers
A denial of service against the model’s API that takes it offline for a while
A backdoor inserted into the target model through its training pipeline
quiz.why: Extraction queries a model and trains a substitute on its outputs, copying functionality without touching the weights.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t encrypting model weights at rest prevent model extraction?
o: Encryption slows the model down so much that attackers have more time to query it
Extraction works through the public API and never touches the stored weights
Encrypted weights are easier to copy, because encryption also compresses them
Attackers can always recover the encryption keys from the API’s responses
quiz.why: Extraction uses legitimate queries and answers. Controls must therefore act on the API: authentication, output minimisation, rate limits and detection.

quiz.q: What is the core difference between a model watermark and a passive fingerprint?
o: A watermark is visible to users, while a fingerprint is always hidden from them
A watermark is embedded on purpose; a passive fingerprint is an existing trait
A watermark proves who trained a model, while a fingerprint proves who used it
A watermark applies only to images, while a fingerprint applies only to text
quiz.why: Watermarks are deliberately embedded signals. Passive fingerprints identify a model from characteristics it already has, without changing it.

quiz.q: Why should a watermark detector’s result be treated as evidence rather than proof?
o: Detectors work only on text written in English, not on other languages
Detection can give false positives, and paraphrasing can weaken watermarks
Courts never accept technical evidence about AI-generated content
Watermarks become invalid as soon as the model is updated to a new version
quiz.why: Detection is statistical and watermarks can be degraded, so results should be combined with logs, contracts and other evidence.

quiz.q: Why is a model package verified with a signed manifest rather than a single file hash?
o: A manifest compresses the model, which makes deployment noticeably faster
Models are usually many files, and the signature covers every file’s digest
A single hash can’t be computed for files larger than four gigabytes
A signed manifest removes the need to keep models in a registry at all
quiz.why: Weight shards, tokenizer and configuration files all shape behaviour. Hashing each one and signing the list protects the whole package.

quiz.q: Which risk is MOST relevant when loading a third-party pickle-based model checkpoint?
o: The checkpoint may take up too much disk space on the inference server
Pickle files can execute arbitrary code at the moment they are loaded
Pickle files hide extra layers that only activate outside office hours
Pickle checkpoints always lose accuracy when they are decompressed
quiz.why: Pickle deserialisation can run code, so untrusted checkpoints should be scanned in a sandbox and converted to a data-only format such as safetensors.

quiz.q: Why should rate limits for LLM APIs count tokens as well as requests?
o: Token counts are easier for customers to understand than request counts
One very long request can use as much capacity as thousands of short ones
Request counts can’t be measured accurately at an API gateway
Tokens are the only unit that model providers allow in their contracts
quiz.why: Cost and capacity scale with tokens, so request-only limits miss resource-heavy prompts and long outputs.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly limits denial-of-wallet attacks on a pay-per-use AI service?
o: A web application firewall that inspects every request for known attack signatures
Per-identity quotas and budget caps that alert and then stop excess usage
Encrypting all prompts in transit with TLS 1.3 between client and API
A longer timeout on the model server, so that requests rarely fail
quiz.why: Denial of wallet exhausts budgets through legitimate-looking use, so quotas and spending caps per identity are the direct control.

quiz.q: What should autoscaling for an AI inference service include, to stay resilient against abuse?
o: No upper limit, so that capacity always matches demand however high it goes
A maximum scale with budget alerts, alongside rate limits and usage quotas
Scaling based only on the number of users who are currently logged in
Manual approval before every scaling event, at any time of day or night
quiz.why: Unlimited autoscaling turns an attack into a cost problem. A ceiling, budget alerts and per-identity limits keep both capacity and spend under control.

exam.q: A start-up fine-tunes an open-weight base model on proprietary customer-service data and serves it from a third-party GPU cloud. The board’s main concern is theft of the fine-tuned weights. Which approach BEST addresses this?
o: Publish the fine-tuned weights openly, since the base model they came from is already open-weight
Encrypt with customer-managed keys, restrict access, and serve in attested confidential computing
Rely on the cloud provider’s standard terms, which state that customer data won’t be accessed
Rename the model files and keep them in an unlisted storage bucket that only the engineering team knows about
exam.why: The fine-tune embodies proprietary data and effort, whatever the base model’s licence. Customer-controlled encryption, least privilege and confidential computing with attestation protect it at rest and in use on infrastructure the start-up doesn’t control. Contract terms and obscurity are not technical controls.

exam.q: Monitoring of a fraud-scoring API shows that three keys belonging to one customer together send two million queries a day with near-random feature values, far more than any other customer. What is the BEST immediate response?
o: Take no action, because the customer is paying for every query that it sends to the API
Throttle the linked keys, investigate the account, and review whether full scores need returning
Retrain the model immediately, so that any copy the customer is building will be out of date
Publish the model openly instead, because extraction can never be fully prevented anyway
exam.why: The pattern (very high volume, synthetic-looking inputs, linked keys) suggests extraction. Throttling contains it, investigation confirms it, and output minimisation reduces future leakage. Paying for queries doesn’t make extraction acceptable, and retraining or publishing is disproportionate.

exam.q: A provider finds that a competitor’s new chatbot gives its model’s planted answers to most of the provider’s secret trigger prompts. What does this MOST strongly indicate, and what should the provider do?
o: Coincidence, since models trained on similar public data usually behave in the same ways
Likely derivation from its model; preserve evidence and pursue legal and contractual remedies
A breach of the provider’s own training data, which must now be deleted and rebuilt at once
That its watermark has failed, so it should be removed from all of the provider’s future models
exam.why: Trigger-set answers far above chance are strong evidence of copying or distillation. The provider should preserve evidence (test results, logs, terms of service) and pursue remedies, treating the watermark as one part of the case.

exam.q: An incident review finds that a production assistant’s system prompt was edited directly on the server six weeks ago, weakening its refusal rules, and nobody knows who made the change. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Encrypting the system prompt at rest on the inference server with a managed key
Managing prompts as code: versioned, peer-reviewed and deployed only through the signed pipeline
Asking the model to report any changes to its own instructions at the start of each reply
A monthly manual comparison of the deployed prompt against a printed copy kept on file
exam.why: Treating prompts as configuration under change control (versioning, review, signed deployment, no direct server edits) prevents unreviewed changes and records who changed what. Encryption doesn’t stop authorised-path edits, and monthly checks only detect problems late.

exam.q: A data science team downloads a popular pre-trained model from a public hub. The files are pickle-based and carry no publisher signature. What should security require BEFORE the model is loaded on internal systems?
o: Nothing further, because popular models on public hubs are reviewed by the community
Scan it in an isolated sandbox, convert it to a safe format, and verify provenance where possible
Load it on one developer’s laptop first, to check whether anything unusual happens
Rename the files with a safe extension, so that internal systems won’t treat them as executable code
exam.why: Pickle files can execute code on load, so untrusted files must be scanned in isolation and converted to a data-only format such as safetensors, with provenance checked (Module 3.7). Popularity isn’t assurance, a laptop isn’t a sandbox, and renaming changes nothing.

exam.q: A public chatbot’s costs triple overnight. Logs show a few accounts repeatedly sending maximum-length prompts and requesting maximum-length answers. Request-count rate limits are in place and weren’t exceeded. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Double the request-count limits, so that legitimate users aren’t affected by any change
Add token-based rate limits, per-identity quotas, output length limits and budget caps
Move every user permanently to a much cheaper model, whatever the impact on quality
Turn the chatbot off until the account holders responsible can be identified in court
exam.why: The abuse used heavy requests, not many requests, so controls must count tokens and cap output, with quotas and budget caps limiting each identity and total spend. Raising limits makes it worse, and the other options are disproportionate.

exam.q: An insurer’s claims-triage assistant depends on a third-party LLM API, which suffers a four-hour outage. Claims must still be triaged within a regulatory deadline. Which resilience design is BEST?
o: Wait for the provider to restore service, because its contract includes a 99.9% availability SLA
A circuit breaker that switches to an approved fallback model, then to a manual triage queue
Switch automatically to whichever public model is cheapest and available at the time
Queue the claims and triage them all once the API returns, accepting the missed deadline
exam.why: Graceful degradation keeps the essential service running: a circuit breaker, a pre-approved fallback model, then a non-AI path. An SLA gives compensation, not continuity, and an unapproved fallback bypasses governance.
